articles.title: Extreme Heat, Not Just Warming, Threatens India’s Rice Crop: Study - Ground Report
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Assam
articles.full_text:
India could lose 6.6 percent of its rice harvest for every 1°C the planet warms — more than triple earlier estimates. Rice feeds nearly two-thirds of the country. The new figure comes from the largest real-world dataset yet built to answer a stubborn question: how much damage does extreme heat, as opposed to average warming, actually do to rice?
The study, published in Science Advances, was led by scientists at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research, with contributions from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. Researchers compared field-warming experiments at 214 sites across rice-growing regions with outputs from seven major crop models used to forecast global food supply.
The gap between the two was stark. Models predicted a 3.8 percent yield loss under 1°C of warming. Real fields lost 8.1 percent — more than double.
Heat Above 30°C Does the Damage
The study pinpoints the cause: exposure to temperatures above 30°C, not rising averages, drives most of the loss. At more than 70 percent of the sites studied, high-temperature exposure alone accounted for over half of the total yield damage recorded.
Lead author Yiwei Jian, a researcher at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research, said existing crop models miss this because they fail to capture heat damage during rice’s reproductive stage — the narrow window when panicles and grains form and the plant is most fragile.
South Asia Faces the Steepest Losses
Regional projections worsened sharply once researchers accounted for real-world heat exposure. For Pakistan, India and Bangladesh, the yield-loss estimate rose from 2.1 to 6.6 percent. For Thailand, the Philippines and Myanmar, it rose from 3.7 to 7.7 percent. South and Southeast Asia now rank as the most exposed rice-growing regions on Earth.
A March analysis in Nature Food warned that half of crop production in low-latitude regions could become unviable once warming crosses 1.5°C. That study projected crop diversity would shrink across 52 percent of global cropland at 2°C of warming, and 56 percent at 3°C.
A May study using six decades of data, from 1966 to 2016, found that each 1°C of warming cut India’s average crop yield by roughly 8 percent nationwide. Pearl millet fell by up to 19 percent. Maize dropped more than 16 percent. In the hardest-hit districts, yields collapsed by as much as 39 percent.
Rice breeders have spent decades optimizing crops for slow, steady warming. This study says that’s the wrong target. The real threat arrives in short, brutal bursts above 30°C — and current forecasting tools aren’t built to see it coming.

Latvia is set for a spell of hot summer weather, with temperatures expected to climb as high as 30°C over the weekend, according to the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Centre.
On Friday, sunshine will alternate with clouds, but the weather will remain dry across the country. With light winds, patches of fog are expected to develop overnight and during the early morning hours in some areas, reducing visibility. Daytime temperatures will reach 23–28°C, although coastal areas will remain a few degrees cooler.
The weather will become more changeable over the weekend. On Saturday, cloud cover will increase, bringing rain to eastern Latvia, while isolated thunderstorms are also expected.
Rain clouds will continue to affect eastern regions during the night into Sunday.
Dry weather is forecast to return on Monday, while Tuesday is expected to bring rain showers to many parts of the country.
Saturday is forecast to be the hottest day of the week, with temperatures rising to 25–30°C. Cooler conditions are expected on Sunday, when daytime highs will range between 20°C and 25°C.

articles.title: UK heatwave map: Where temperatures will be highest today in ‘North-South split’ - independent.co.uk

articles.full_text:
Parts of southern England are basking in a fourth heatwave this week, with high temperatures set to continue until the weekend.
The Environment Agency have warned that swathes of the country are now officially in drought as a result of very low rainfall, with farmers warning of low produce.
The latest UK heatwave peaked on Wednesday with temperatures soaring to 35.2C at Writtle in Essex, with the coming days unlikely to bring any rain for the south of England.
Amber heat health alerts were issued from 9am on Wednesday to 9am on Thursday for the East Midlands, London, the south-east and east of England. Yorkshire and the Humber, the West Midlands and south-west England are all under yellow alerts.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) issued a warning of possible “significant impacts” on health and social care services, including a rise in deaths among the elderly or people with health conditions, and an increase in drownings.
Three heatwaves have already been recorded across the country since May, with temperatures breaking records in June, as the UK faces more extreme weather fuelled by human-caused climate change.
On Wednesday, temperatures reached 33C in London and surrounding counties, with highs of 25C recorded in Manchester and 26C in Cardiff.
The hot weather will continue into Thursday but will remain cooler in the North, with highs of 19C recorded in Belfast and 18C in Glasgow.
Forecasters are expecting this week’s heat to be a “North-South split”, with clouds and outbreaks of rain continuing in Northern Ireland, Scotland and northern England.
But the peak will be “almost a blink and you miss it”, with temperatures widely cooling close to average by the weekend, said senior Met Office meteorologist Dan Stroud.
From Friday, temperatures are expected to be much closer to average across most of the UK, and even slightly below average for northern Scotland.
Saturday will have a chilly start for many, but there will be lots of dry weather with some sunny spells, with Reading expected to enjoy temperatures of 25C and Nottingham set for 22C.
July was 3C above average across the UK, according to provisional Met Office data.
This could put it among the hottest three or four months of July on record, said senior Met Office meteorologist Dan Stroud. Some parts of the UK had rain over the weekend, mainly in the North and North West, with 33mm (1.3in) falling on Sunday at Charterhall, in the Scottish Borders, and Altnahinch Filters in Co Antrim, Northern Ireland, receiving 17mm (0.7in).
But mainly places missed out and stayed largely dry, the Met Office said, with little, if any, relief in some southern regions.
Some spots have gone for weeks without rain – such as Wisley in Surrey, which has had 40 consecutive dry days.
The heat and ongoing dry conditions have led to hosepipe bans for 23 million customers, while even water companies without bans in place are telling households to conserve water, and drought has been declared across a swathe of Wales.
Southern England has had just one per cent of its average July rainfall. England has had five per cent and the UK as a whole 20 per cent, according to the Met Office.
However, the forecaster warned that heatwave thresholds will need to be adjusted to take into account the warming climate, with fire chiefs also warning of the additional risk of wildfires.
At the height of the third heatwave, in mid-July, firefighters were battling 19 significant wildfires simultaneously in England and Wales.
A National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) spokesperson said: “With the Met Office warning that a fourth heatwave could develop this week, bringing another period of very hot weather to parts of the UK, fire and rescue services remain on alert and are continuing to prepare for renewed wildfire risk.”
The dry spell has contributed to low water levels, and north Wales and the Upper Severn became the first part of the UK to declare drought status on Thursday.
Fires, if they start, are likely to become exceptionally severe in pockets of the East, South, and south-east England, according to Met Office data used by Natural England and Natural Resources Wales.
The “exceptionally severe” warnings focus on eastern England on Thursday.
Met Office chief meteorologist, Dan Suri, said: "After a prolonged spell of hot, dry and settled weather, some will see a temporary change this weekend as weather fronts move south-east across the UK.
“While some areas, particularly in the North and West, will see rain and showers, many places are likely to receive relatively little rainfall.
“For much of southern England, dry conditions are expected to remain the dominant feature, with temperatures recovering quickly next week and the potential for very warm or locally hot weather to return."
Met Office five-day weather forecast
Thursday
Cloud and patchy rain will move south-eastwards across England and Wales. Less warm than recently here too. Elsewhere it will be fresher with more in the way of sunshine, though it will be windy across Scotland with blustery showers.
Thursday night
Patchy cloud giving a few early evening showers across south-east England. Clear periods elsewhere. However, some cloud, and breezy in the North and North West, with some showers. Fresher for all.
Friday
Mostly dry in the South and South East on Friday with some warm spells of sunshine. Cooler, with a breeze towards the north and northwest, and a scattering of showers.
Saturday to Monday
Remaining breezy with showers in the North on Saturday. Largely dry with warm sunshine further South. Most places dry on Sunday, then showers could break out more widely on Monday.

JINCHANG, China, July 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- State Grid Gansu Jinchang Power Supply Company has launched a targeted safety inspection and power service for the construction site of Gansu Jinhui Agricultural Product Deep Processing Project, to secure stable and safe power consumption amid persistent summer high temperatures.
As scorching weather drives a sharp rise in power demand for construction and operational activities, temporary electrical facilities at the project site face heightened risks including equipment overload, accelerated aging and operational faults. To mitigate potential hazards and ensure reliable power supply during the critical construction phase, the company's professional team conducted a comprehensive on-site inspection focusing on core temporary power facilities.
During the field check, inspectors thoroughly examined key operational indicators of on-site transformers and essential electrical equipment, covering operating temperature, load capacity, wiring systems, earthing protection and insulation conditions. All hidden dangers such as equipment overheating and circuit aging were screened out, and real-time operational parameters under high-temperature conditions were fully recorded to establish a standardized hazard investigation ledger. For minor irregularities identified on site, technicians provided on-the-spot guidance for rectification. Meanwhile, they delivered professional guidance on daily equipment maintenance, standard power usage specifications and emergency response protocols for hot weather, further consolidating the site's electrical safety foundation.
As a pivotal local project for upgrading characteristic agricultural industries, the organic fruit and vegetable juice deep processing project undertaken by Gansu Jinhui Agricultural Processing Co., Ltd. boasts outstanding industrial driving potential. Upon completion and operation, the project will deploy fully automatic assembly lines covering cleaning, sorting, pressing and pulping processes. It will introduce the province's first aseptic cold filling production line with an hourly output of 24,000 bottles, building Gansu's professional and high-standard fruit and vegetable aseptic cold filling production base.
The project will fill the local gap in intensive processing of fruit and vegetable agricultural products, extend the agricultural industrial chain and raise product added value. It will also drive the local modern agriculture toward industrialization, large-scale development and high-quality upgrading, injecting strong impetus into regional agricultural economic development.

articles.title: New guidance targets exertional heat stroke in high school football linemen - WKYT
articles.search_term: (heatstroke OR "heat stroke" OR sunstroke OR "heat exhaustion" OR "heat-related death" OR "heat casualty" OR "heat fatality" OR "suspected heat death" OR dehydration OR "heat cramps" OR "heat illness") Assam
articles.full_text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - According to the National Federation of State High School Associations (NFHS), exertional heat stroke (EHS) is the number one cause of preventable death in youth, high school, and collegiate football players.
History of EHS in Football Players
The first recorded EHS death in the modern era of football was David Tilson, a high schooler, in 1955. From 1955 through 2021, the National Registry of Catastrophic Sports Injuries documented 159 EHS fatalities.
Deaths started to decline in the 1960s, with the introduction of prevention strategies such as reducing the uniform from full pads to shorts and T-shirts and practicing in the cool of the day. There was an added focus on hydration, but the deaths continued.
The 2001 football EHS deaths of NFL player Korey Stringer, NCAA player Eraste Autin, and high schooler Travis Stowers led to the development of more training guidelines from the NCAA and the American Football Coaches Association. Despite these efforts, there were 14 youth, high school, and college football EHS fatalities in the 2020-21 season alone.
Linemen are Most At-Risk
In order to reduce EHS deaths in high schoolers, the NFHS Sports Medicine Advisory Committee (SMAC) convened an expert task force that consisted of physicians, athletic trainers, state association executives, athletic directors, football coaches, and strength and conditioning coaches.
The task force found that 100 percent of high school and college football deaths from exertional heat stroke occur during conditioning sessions, often within the first week of practice. Ninety-seven percent of those deaths involve linemen. According to SMAC, linemen tend to heat up faster, cool down more slowly, and “face unique physiological risks not fully mitigated by existing guidelines on hydration, acclimation, WBGT monitoring, or uniform modification.
Local coach focuses on hydration, sleep, and acclimation
Fredrick Douglass High School football coach Nate McPeek said prevention starts before players arrive at practice.
“The first thing is talking to our kids about sleep, hydration, eating before they arrive each practice,” McPeek said. “Obviously, we hydrate during practice and after practice. The biggest thing in the heat is just make sure the kids and the parents are aware that they need to eat something. And obviously, sleep — seven to nine hours — is super important.”
McPeek said he structures practice length to allow players to gradually adjust to the heat.
“You may get an hour of work, and then an hour and a half, and then an hour and 40 minutes, and you build it up,” McPeek said. “But I’m not a huge two-hour practice guy. I never have been. We’re an hour and 45 minutes of work.”
All players are monitored for hydration during practice, and McPeek said every staff member watches for signs of heat-related illness.
Preventing EHS
The NFHS SMAC Task Force shared the EHS statistics and information with all KHSAA contacts involved in football, along with new, position-specific guidance.
The following recommendations were included:
Position-specific training and conditioning, with a gradual and paced progression in intensity and duration.
Continue well-established guidelines for heat acclimatization, hydration, and WBGT scales.
Exclude linemen from certain preseason performance testing, such as mile runs, during the first few weeks of practice.
Never use exertion drills as punishment, as this accounts for 37% of football EHS deaths.
Withdraw struggling athletes from training and conditioning for evaluation and treatment.
Rehearse the EHS Emergency Action Plan (EAP) with rapid cooling protocols.
According to SMAC, EHS tends to be caused by exercise intensity more than environmental factors.
Signs of Exertional Heat Stroke
According to the Cleveland Clinic, heat stroke occurs when heat overwhelms your body’s ability to manage its temperature. Untreated heat exhaustion can lead to heat stroke. Both have symptoms that include dizziness, nausea, and weakness. One key difference is that heat stroke can cause changes to your thinking and behavior, such as confusion, agitation, and aggression.
Exertional heat stroke typically affects young, healthy adults and often occurs when physical activity and hot weather mix.
Other symptoms of heat stroke include:
Fever (over 104 degrees Fahrenheit)
Fast heart rate
Fast, shallow breathing
Low blood pressure
Seizures
Blurred vision
Slurred speech
Skin color changes (flushed or paler than usual)
If you or someone around you has signs or symptoms of heat stroke, call 911 immediately.

Samsung Q2 results: Tech giant's revenue reaches all-time high of $119 billion amid strong semiconductor demand Technology giant Samsung Electronics posted a record operating profit for the quarter ended June 30, while its revenue reached an all-time high of 171.5 trillion won ($119 billion), driven by its semiconductor business. South Korea-based technology giant Samsung Electronics on Thursday reported a record operating profit of 89.5 trillion won ($62 billion) for the quarter ended June. The tech giant follows the calendar year for its financial reporting, with the first quarter running from January to March, the second from April to June, the third from July to September, and the fourth from October to December. Its fiscal year ends on December 31. The technology giant reported a more than 19-fold jump in operating profit for the second quarter compared with the same period last year. According to AP, the majority of its earnings came from the company's semiconductor division, which benefited from rising chip prices driven by robust demand for AI servers and higher shipments of advanced high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Further, the semiconductor division's strong performance offset an operating loss in the company's mobile, TV and home appliances business, where higher component costs weighed on profitability. Samsung's second-quarter revenue reached an all-time high of 171.5 trillion won ($119 billion). The company said it expects robust demand for memory products in the second half of the year, driven by the expansion of AI infrastructure and the broader adoption of agentic AI. It also said growing demand for server chips is expected to keep the memory chip market undersupplied. The results came a day after rival SK Hynix posted record earnings, as the world's two biggest memory chipmakers continue to benefit from surging demand driven by the AI boom. SK Hynix posts record earnings but shares fall On Tuesday, SK Hynix also reported record earnings, with its second-quarter revenue reaching 60.5 trillion won ($42 billion). However, the company's profit remained below market expectations, with its shares declining by over nine per cent on Wednesday. Meanwhile, Samsung's shares have also declined this week. Shares of the world's two largest memory chipmakers fell in South Korea's volatile stock market, where retail investors often trigger sharp price swings, amid growing concerns over the companies' aggressive manufacturing expansion plans and the prospect of intensifying competition from Chinese rivals. Further, shares of the two rival chipmakers have also been under pressure amid growing concerns over intensifying competition from China, with reports suggesting that a state-owned Beijing company has now commenced mass production of advanced immersion deep-ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines, a key technology for advanced chipmaking, domestically. Additionally, investors have also been buoyed by the strong stock market debut of ChangXin Memory Technologies, a Chinese memory chipmaker. Concerns grow over Samsung, SK Hynix's soaring investments According to reports, the two rivals together produce roughly two-thirds of the world's memory chips, and while the companies have announced plans for major investments in semiconductor manufacturing facilities and data centres, there are growing concerns over whether such massive spending will ultimately generate sufficient returns. This comes after both Samsung and SK Hynix announced plans last month to invest a combined 800 trillion won ($554 billion) in a new chipmaking hub in the country’s southwest to capitalize on surging AI-driven demand. The heads of Samsung, SK Group and South Korean automaker Hyundai accompanied President Lee Jae Myung on his visit to San Francisco last week, where they unveiled plans for hundreds of billions of dollars in collaborations with leading US technology companies, including AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as chip designers Nvidia and Broadcom. The partnerships cover chip technologies, data centres and other AI infrastructure. Swati Gandhi is a digital journalist with over four years of experience, specialising in international and geopolitical issues. Covering multiple beats early in her career has helped her be informed about her current work, allowing her to connect domestic developments with wider international trends.

Monsoon lull to end in Mumbai, Thane? IMD issues yellow alert - check forecast
An orange alert covering extremely heavy rainfall has been sounded for Raigad, the ghat areas of Pune, Kolhapur and Satara, besides Nashik, Dhule, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Jalna, Amravati, Wardha, Nagpur, Bhandara, Gondia, Chandrapur and Gadchiroli, as per IMD.
Mumbai and its neighbouring regions are bracing for a fresh spell of heavy rain and thunderstorms starting Thursday, July 30, after a brief lull in monsoon activity, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).
The weather office has upgraded its warning for the city to yellow, citing thunderstorms accompanied by lightning, heavy rainfall and gusty winds of 50 to 60 kmph at isolated places.
Thane is likely to witness similar conditions on Thursday, with thunderstorms and heavy rain forecast through the day. Neighbouring Palghar district has been placed under an orange alert for Friday, July 31. The warning points to heavy to very heavy rainfall, thunderstorms with lightning and gusty winds of 50 to 60 kmph at isolated places.
Several other Maharashtra districts have also been placed on alert as the monsoon shows signs of revival. Jalgaon has been issued a red alert, warning of heavy rainfall conditions.
An orange alert covering extremely heavy rainfall has been sounded for Raigad, the ghat areas of Pune, Kolhapur and Satara, besides Nashik, Dhule, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Jalna, Amravati, Wardha, Nagpur, Bhandara, Gondia, Chandrapur and Gadchiroli, as per IMD.
A yellow alert, meanwhile, is in force for Mumbai, Thane, Palghar, Nandurbar, Ratnagiri, Sindhudurg, Satara, Pune, Beed, Parbhani, Latur, Nanded, Hingoli, Buldhana, Akola, Washim and Yavatmal, with heavy rain expected across these districts.
Meteorologists have linked the renewed monsoon activity to a deep depression system over Odisha, which has strengthened rainfall patterns across the region, the report stated.
Mumbai had been experiencing a lull in rainfall in recent days, driven by the absence of active monsoon systems following a spell of above normal rain through July.
Data furnished by the IMD shows that between Tuesday, July 28, and Wednesday morning, July 29, the Colaba coastal observatory recorded 4.8 mm of rain, while the Santacruz station registered just 0.1 mm, the report said. This came after the eastern suburbs recorded an average of 8 mm rainfall, followed by around 3 mm across the western suburbs and the island city.
So far, Mumbai's suburbs have recorded 1,490 mm of rainfall in July, considerably higher than the city's actual monthly quota, the report added.

articles.full_text:
Storms: Île-de-France on yellow alert this Thursday
Published by
Caroline de Sortiraparis · Photos by
My de Sortiraparis · Updated on July 30, 2026 at 08:28 a.m.
Even as it remained very hot across the country on Wednesday, Météo France announced the arrival of thunderstorms and placed several departments across the Hexagon under a yellow alert for Thursday, July 30, 2026. All departments in Île-de-France are now included in this yellow alert. Here’s the latest.
People are already worn out after three back-to-back heatwaves. Since Tuesday, temperatures have risen again nationwide, and a new heatwave has struck France on this July 29. On Wednesday, temperatures frequently topped 37°C in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, Occitanie, Auvergne, the Rhône and Saône valleys, Burgundy, and even Île-de-France.
We note that France endured from July 4 to 19 its second heatwave of the summer, notably gruelling because of its duration (15 days). "Only the summers of 2017 and 2022 have seen three heatwaves. In 2017, they were short (3 or 4 days). In 2022, France faced a short heatwave in June (5 days) and two long ones in July and August (14 days each)", explains Météo France.
Yellow alert for potential thunderstorms across the Île-de-France region
So what should we expect in the days ahead? Thursday, July 30, temperatures are expected to drop noticeably in the west, "however the heat should persist over a large part of the east of France," according to Météo France. On Thursday and Friday, thunderstorms, "whose intensity is uncertain at this stage," will sweep across the country and help cool things down.
This Thursday, Météo France has placed about forty departments on yellow alert for possible thunderstorms. In Île-de-France, the entire region is now under the yellow alert, namely Paris and the inner suburbs (the Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne), but also Essonne, the Seine-et-Marne, the Yvelines and the Val-d'Oise. According to the meteorological service, these thundery showers could hit the capital and its surroundings on Thursday morning until roughly 1 p.m.
What's more, winds will also gust through parts of Île-de-France, with gusts reaching up to about 60 km/h on Thursday morning, notably in the eastern part of Seine-et-Marne.
What to do during thunderstorms?
Because of this yellow "thunderstorms" alert issued by Météo-France, it is important to remind everyone of the usual safety guidelines, such as avoiding outdoor activities, not taking shelter under trees or under an overhang, and not driving on flooded roads.
